items.caption: Interactive UMAP co-embedding of all 4,096 A/1 features and all 512 A/0 features, with a searchable cluster/feature list beside it.
items.focus: Explain that the left pane is a scrollable list grouped into numbered clusters, each row a feature id (A/0/307, A/1/776 …) plus its short human label, and the right pane a 2-D UMAP scatter of those same features where proximity means similar activation behaviour and labelled points are the cluster exemplars. Note the axes are UMAP coordinates with no units, and that the [Ultralow density cluster] label marks the dead/ultralow-density features.

items.caption: Schematic of the one-layer transformer with the MLP activations singled out for decomposition into features.
items.focus: Cover the whole data path drawn — token embedding, attention layer, MLP with its 512 neurons, unembedding — and make clear that only the post-ReLU MLP activation vector is fed to the autoencoder, and why that is the layer that cannot be avoided.

items.caption: Correspondence between the transformer and the sparse autoencoder (feature counts and expansion factors).
items.focus: Walk every row and both columns: the Transformer column (layers, MLP width 512 neurons, 8 billion training activations) against the Sparse Autoencoder column (hidden dimension = 512 × expansion factor, from 1× = 512 features up to 256× = 131,072 features, with 8× / 4,096 features as the run A/1 the paper analyses in depth). State the units of every number.

items.caption: Superposition as 'noisy simulation': a small dense network approximately simulating a larger, sparser one.
items.focus: Explain both networks drawn side by side — the small observed network with few neurons and the hypothetical large sparse network with many features — the arrow meaning 'approximately simulates', and why feature sparsity plus high-dimensional almost-orthogonality is what makes the simulation possible with interference noise.

items.caption: The per-feature visualization interface: activating dataset examples, logit effects, and activation distribution.
items.focus: Name each panel of the interface screenshot — top activating dataset examples with orange activation shading, the logit-weight lists of up- and down-weighted tokens, the activation histogram, and the subsampled-interval examples — and say what a reader should read off each.

items.caption: Feature search interface.
items.focus: Describe the search box, what is being matched (feature labels/explanations), and the result rows returned, so a reader understands this is a lookup tool over the 4,096 features rather than an analysis result.

items.caption: Data-oriented interface showing all features active on each token of a dataset example.
items.focus: Explain that the rows are tokens of one text and the entries are the features firing on that token with their activation magnitudes, i.e. the transpose of the per-feature view, and why this makes the sparsity per token visible.

items.caption: Introduction of the computational proxy used to test whether a feature fires only in a rare, specific context.
items.focus: Cover what the proxy is a proxy for (log-likelihood ratio that a string comes from the hypothesised context), what is on each axis, and the logic that high specificity rules out the usual form of polysemanticity.

items.caption: Arabic feature A/1/3450: fraction of activation attributable to Arabic script, broken down by feature activity level (25% when barely active up to ~81% at high activation).
items.focus: Give the x-axis (feature activation level, binned from just-above-zero to maximum), the y-axis (percentage of tokens in that bin that are Arabic script), the two named endpoint numbers, and the interpretive point that specificity rises sharply with activation strength.

items.caption: Activation distribution of the Arabic feature coloured by the Arabic-script proxy, showing where the magnitude of activation comes from.
items.focus: Explain the histogram's x-axis (activation value), y-axis (density or count), and the colour encoding of the proxy score, plus the claim it supports: most of the total activation mass sits on Arabic-script examples.

items.caption: Logit weights of the Arabic feature, showing a second mode of Arabic characters and Arabic-script continuation tokens.
items.focus: Describe the logit-weight histogram over the whole vocabulary, the bulk 'interference' mode near zero and the separated positive mode, and that the tokens in that second mode are Arabic characters — this is the downstream-effect evidence.

items.caption: Ablation effects of the Arabic feature on next-token log-likelihood, larger where the feature is more active.
items.focus: Cover the token-level display: orange background for feature activation, blue underline for the ablation effect on the following token's log-likelihood, and the monotone relation between activation magnitude and ablation impact.

items.caption: Samples generated with A/1/3450 pinned to its maximum observed value.
items.focus: State the intervention (feature clamped to max during a forward pass), what the sampled text looks like as a result (Arabic script), and that this is the sufficiency half of the causal argument, complementing ablation.

items.caption: Coefficients of the Arabic feature in the neuron basis; the three largest coefficients are highlighted.
items.focus: Give the axis meaning (one bar per one of the 512 MLP neurons, height = that neuron's coefficient in the feature's dictionary vector), point out that no single neuron dominates, and name the top-3 neurons as the ones followed up in the next figures.

items.caption: Activation distribution of the top neuron, showing it fires on many non-Arabic dataset examples.
items.focus: Explain the neuron activation histogram and the coloured dataset examples, and the contrast being drawn: the neuron is polysemantic where the feature is specific.

items.caption: Neuron logit weights on Arabic-script tokens — slightly positive on average, but many negative.
items.focus: Cover the token-level weight display, the sign pattern described, and why a weak mixed signal is evidence the neuron is not the Arabic feature.

items.caption: Joint scatter of feature activation against neuron activation with x- and y-marginals.
items.focus: Name both axes (feature activation vs neuron activation), explain the marginal histograms drawn on each edge, and the paper's reading: the y-marginal (feature) shows clean specificity while the x-marginal (neuron) does not.

items.caption: Feature B/1/1334, the highest activation-correlated match to the Arabic feature in an independently trained run (corr = 0.91).
items.focus: Cover what run B is (a second transformer + autoencoder trained from a different seed), how the match was found (maximum activation correlation), and the 0.91 value.

items.caption: Activation display for B/1/1334 showing it responds to Arabic script, arguably more cleanly than the A/1 feature.
items.focus: Describe the dataset-example panel and activation shading, and the universality claim it supports: two independent runs recover the same feature.

items.caption: Scatter plots comparing activations and logit weights between runs A and B for the Arabic feature.
items.focus: Name both scatter panels — activation correlation across shared tokens, and logit-weight correlation across the vocabulary — give the axes (A value vs B value) and note the asymmetry the text emphasises (high activation correlation, much lower logit-weight correlation, 0.23).

items.caption: DNA feature A/1/2937: binarized [ATCG] proxy has Pearson correlation 0.8 with feature activations.
items.focus: Explain the proxy (string modelled as random draws from A/T/C/G, binarized), the axes of the comparison, and the 0.8 Pearson figure as the specificity evidence.

items.caption: Grid of random dataset examples at four activation levels for the DNA feature, including feature-off.
items.focus: State that the grid rows are activation quantiles (off, low, medium, high) and the cells are randomly sampled examples at that level, so a reader can see specificity increase down the grid and spot the cases where the proxy and the feature disagree.

items.caption: Logit weights of the DNA feature — the top up-weighted tokens are DNA-related.
items.focus: Cover the ranked token list, what a logit weight is (the feature direction pushed through the unembedding), and that all top tokens are nucleotide strings.

items.caption: A/neurons/227, the highest-coefficient neuron for the DNA feature, shows no DNA sequences in its top examples.
items.focus: Describe the neuron's top-activating examples panel and make explicit the negative result: the closest neuron is not a DNA detector.

items.caption: B/1/3680, the DNA feature's match in run B (corr = 0.92), with agreeing top logit weights.
items.focus: Cover the paired activation and logit displays, the 0.92 correlation, and that the agreement is on DNA tokens specifically.

items.caption: base64 feature A/1/2357: activation distribution coloured by the base64 proxy, alongside random dataset examples.
items.focus: Give the histogram axes, the proxy colouring, and the sampled examples panel, and the specificity conclusion for base64 strings.

items.caption: Conditional view showing a continuous transition to base64-specific tokens as activation rises.
items.focus: Explain that this conditions on activation level and plots the proportion of base64 tokens, and why 'continuous transition' rather than a sharp threshold matters for the monosemanticity claim.

items.caption: B/1/2165, the base64 feature's match in run B (corr = 0.85), with high activation specificity.
items.focus: Cover the matched-feature display and the 0.85 correlation as universality evidence for base64.

items.caption: B/1/2165 logit weights showing a second mode of base64 tokens.
items.focus: Describe the bimodal logit-weight histogram and identify the tokens in the separated mode.

items.caption: Activation and logit-weight correlation scatter plots between A/1/2357 and B/1/2165.
items.focus: Name both scatter axes (run A value vs run B value, over shared tokens and over the vocabulary respectively) and report what agreement level each shows.

items.caption: A/neurons/470 (corr 0.18): responds to base64 strings but also to unrelated inputs.
items.focus: Cover the neuron's activation display and the mixed set of contexts it fires on — the polysemanticity contrast that makes the feature/neuron distinction.

items.caption: Logit weights of A/neurons/470, focused mostly on non-base64 tokens.
items.focus: Explain the ranked token weights and the point that the neuron's downstream effect is not base64-specific.

items.caption: Activation and logit correlations for A/neurons/470, consistent with it helping represent the base64 feature without being it.
items.focus: Give both scatter axes and the interpretation: partial, noisy alignment rather than identity — the neuron carries part of the feature in superposition.

items.caption: Hebrew feature A/1/416 activation distribution coloured by proxy, with blue at strong activations on common characters.
items.focus: Explain the colour scale (proxy score, blue = low/common characters), the x-axis of activation, and the caveat the colouring reveals about shared punctuation.

items.caption: Token-level view noting that \xd7 is the first byte-token of most basic-block Hebrew characters.
items.focus: Cover the tokenizer detail — Hebrew characters are multi-token in UTF-8 and the feature fires on the leading byte token — and why that complicates the proxy.

items.caption: Activation and logit correlation plots for the Hebrew feature against its nearest neuron.
items.focus: Name both axes and state the conclusion that no neuron matches the Hebrew feature.

items.caption: B/1/1901, the Hebrew feature's match in run B (corr = 0.92).
items.focus: Cover the matched feature's activation specificity and the 0.92 figure.

items.caption: Logit weights of the Hebrew feature's run-B match, again bimodal.
items.focus: Describe the bimodal histogram and the Hebrew tokens in the second mode.

items.caption: Activation and logit-weight correlation scatters for the Hebrew feature across runs.
items.focus: Give the two panels' axes and their correlation values, closing the universality argument for the fourth case study.

items.caption: Manual human interpretability scoring: 412 features and neurons rated on the paper's rubric.
items.focus: Cover the rubric scale (0–3, see Appendix 14), which populations are compared (autoencoder features vs MLP neurons), the sample size of 412, and the caveat that the sample is small because scoring is labour intensive.

items.caption: Automated interpretability by activation prediction: Claude explains and predicts feature activations far better than neuron activations.
items.focus: Give the x-axis (correlation between Claude's predicted and true activations), the y-axis (density), the two overlaid distributions (features vs neurons) with their medians and means, and the random-chance reference line.

items.caption: Automated interpretability scored on logit weights, with format failures reported.
items.focus: Explain the same distribution layout as the activation version but scored against logit weights, and define 'failures' as cases where Claude did not reply in the parseable format rather than as wrong answers.

items.caption: Activation interval analysis: interpretability as a function of feature activation strength.
items.focus: Give the x-axis (activation interval / quantile of non-zero activations), the y-axis (interpretability score), and the finding that interpretability is highest at strong activations and degrades near zero.

items.caption: Pinned feature sampling: a feature clamped high, then the model sampled.
items.focus: State the intervention, the sampled text shown, and the question it is answering — whether features describe the model's computation or merely the data distribution.

items.caption: UMAP co-embedding of features from runs A/0 (512), A/1 (4,096) and A/2 (16,384), with Arabic-script, base64 and ultralow-density/dead-neuron regions annotated.
items.focus: Cover the legend precisely — large grey = A/0's 512 features, dark green = A/1's 4,096, small light green = A/2's 16,384 — that the axes are unitless UMAP coordinates, and the three text annotations with their arrows; the visual claim is that a coarse A/0 feature sits at the centre of a cloud of finer A/1 and A/2 features, i.e. feature splitting, and that the isolated right-hand blob is ultralow-density and dead neurons.

items.caption: Schematic of feature splitting: as the number of learned sparse features increases, one dictionary direction splits into several with small angles between them.
items.focus: Explain the three panels left-to-right as increasing dictionary size (labelled 'Increasing number of learned sparse features' with a 'Features Split →' arrow), the grey blob as the region of activation space being covered, and the arrows as dictionary vectors — few coarse vectors becoming more, narrowly separated ones.

items.caption: Feature specificity as a function of dictionary size — runs with more learned sparse features are more specific.
items.focus: Give the x-axis (number of learned sparse features / expansion factor), the y-axis (specificity measure), and the monotone trend plus its exceptions.

items.caption: Coarse dictionaries cannot distinguish two concepts that finer dictionaries separate.
items.focus: Name the two concepts being conflated, show which run merges them and which splits them, and tie it back to the splitting mechanism in fig-45.

items.caption: A single A/0 feature splitting into three A/1 features whose activations jointly cover it.
items.focus: Identify the parent feature and the three children, explain 'jointly cover' (union of the children's activations reconstructs the parent's), and what distinguishes the children.

items.caption: A digit-context feature: if the present token is digits, the model predicts a non-digit next token.
items.focus: Cover the activating examples, the logit weights that implement the prediction, and why this looked like a bug before it was understood.

items.caption: Top dataset examples for A/1/1544, showing the particular substrings it fires on.
items.focus: State the substring pattern, the activation shading, and the resolution of the apparent bug it explains.

items.caption: The two notions of cross-model similarity (activation similarity and logit-weight similarity) as correlations of the points in two scatter plots.
items.focus: Define both similarity measures precisely — correlation of per-token activations across models, and correlation of per-vocabulary-token logit weights — and show which scatter each is computed from.

items.caption: Comparison of neurons between two transformers, showing much less similarity (median activation correlation 0.46).
items.focus: Give the distribution's axes, the 0.46 median, and the contrast with the much higher feature-to-feature correlations — the core universality result.

items.caption: Scatterplot showing widespread disagreement between activation similarity and logit-weight similarity.
items.focus: Name both axes (activation correlation vs logit-weight correlation, one point per matched feature pair), and highlight the extreme case A/1/3949 vs B/1/3321 (activation corr 0.98, negative logit corr) discussed in the text.

items.caption: Attribution similarity correlates highly with activation similarity.
items.focus: Define the attribution vector (activation times the logit weight of the token that actually came next), give both scatter axes, and the conclusion that co-active features across models really do predict the same tokens.

items.caption: A base64 feature raising the probability of plausible base64 continuation tokens such as Qg and zA.
items.focus: Cover the token list and weights, and the point that the feature's output re-triggers base64 context — the first half of the finite-state-automaton loop.

items.caption: Two-node system producing all-caps snake case variables (e.g. ARRAY_MAX_VALUE).
items.focus: Explain the two nodes as two features, the transitions as one feature's logit output making the other's activating token likely, and the example string that the loop generates.

items.caption: Two features, one firing on complete characters or the suffix, predicting either continuation.
items.focus: Name each feature, what token it fires on, and which continuation it up-weights, so the state machine's branching is explicit.

items.caption: The full finite-state-automaton system diagram.
items.focus: Walk every node (feature) and every labelled edge (the token whose prediction moves the system to the next state), and state that the automaton is emergent from the feature logit weights, not built in.

items.caption: Contextual IRC-related features forming a similar system.
items.focus: Identify the features and the IRC log formatting they track, showing that these automata are contextual rather than purely lexical.

items.caption: Features tracking standard legal boilerplate found in open-source file headers.
items.focus: Cover the features and the license-header text they cycle through, and why a highly stereotyped corpus region produces a clean automaton.

items.caption: Feature manifolds: structures not well described by one-dimensional features.
items.focus: Explain the geometric sketch — points on a curve/surface in activation space rather than a single direction — and the theoretical worry it raises about the paper's 1-D feature assumption.

items.caption: Two sketches: feature manifolds as correlated features, and structures with no 'correct' set of 1-D features.
items.focus: Describe both panels — the left arc with a few points, the right ring with solid and hollow points — and their captions: some manifold hypotheses reduce to correlated features, while ring-like structures admit no privileged decomposition into one-dimensional features.

items.caption: Kurtosis evidence that the neuron basis is still privileged, from external comments and replications.
items.focus: Give the axis being measured (kurtosis of activations in the neuron basis vs random rotations), and the conclusion that a privileged basis survives despite polysemanticity.

items.caption: Bimodal feature density histogram for a run.
items.focus: Give the x-axis (log feature density, i.e. fraction of tokens on which the feature fires, typically 1e-3 to 1e-6), the y-axis (count of features), and name the two modes: the interpretable low-density cluster and the ultralow-density cluster.

items.caption: The two density clusters are often perfectly separable in small runs but overlap in larger ones.
items.focus: Explain the overlaid histograms per run and the trend with scale, plus why separability matters for filtering dead/ultralow features.

items.caption: The high-density cluster is clearly separable along three dimensions.
items.focus: Name all three axes/dimensions used for the separation and how the clusters occupy them.

items.caption: As the number of autoencoder neurons increases, more features and more ultralow-density neurons are discovered.
items.focus: Give the x-axis (number of learned sparse features), the y-axis (count of features in each cluster), and both curves — real features and ultralow-density ones — since the ratio is the practical concern.

items.caption: Hyperparameter selection: L0 norm and reconstructed-transformer NLL as a human-interpretable tradeoff.
items.focus: Give both axes explicitly — average L0 (number of features active per token) against the negative log-likelihood of the transformer when the MLP is replaced by the autoencoder reconstruction — the direction of the Pareto frontier, and how the L1 coefficient λ moves a run along it.

items.caption: Alternative correlation measure giving distributions and conclusions almost identical to Spearman.
items.focus: State which measure is substituted, that both feature and neuron distributions are shown, and that the robustness check changes nothing.

items.caption: Randomized-transformer features are distinctly bimodal, consisting of single-token and positional features.
items.focus: Give the distribution axes, name the two modes (single-token features and positional features), and the control's purpose: showing that a random transformer yields degenerate features unlike the trained one.

items.caption: Importance-sampled automated interpretability: Spearman correlation density for features (median 0.28, mean 0.35, 0/3676 failures) vs neurons (median 0.04, mean 0.11, 0/512 failures).
items.focus: Cover the x-axis (Spearman correlation, −0.2 to 1.0), the y-axis (density), the two overlaid histograms with their colour legend and both stat boxes including sample sizes, the 'random chance' marker at 0 and the two median triangles. Explain why importance weighting pushes many feature scores toward zero (almost all weight lands on random examples where features rarely fire) and why neurons are less affected.

items.caption: Explanation-length caveat: scores split out by explanation length do not differ significantly.
items.focus: Give the grouping variable (length of Claude's explanation), the score on the y-axis, and the null result being reported.

items.caption: Linear feature decomposition of the MLP activation vector (unnumbered display, Section 2.1 'Features as a Decomposition').
items.focus: Cover every symbol: x^j the d_MLP-dimensional MLP activation vector for datapoint j, f_i(x^j) the scalar activation of feature i, d_i the unit-norm direction of feature i in activation space, and b the bias. Explain why the sum runs over more features than dimensions (overcompleteness), and that this is just a linear matrix factorization of the kind used in dictionary learning.

items.caption: Feature activations as the encoder output, f_i(x) = ReLU(W_e(x − b_d) + b_e)_i (unnumbered display, Section 2.1).
items.focus: Explain each term: W_e the encoder weight matrix, b_d the pre-encoder bias subtracted from the input (tied to the negative of the decoder bias), b_e the encoder bias, and ReLU as what forces non-negative, sparse activations. Say why the feature directions are the columns of W_d rather than rows of W_e.

items.caption: Full sparse autoencoder forward pass and training objective (aligned display, Appendix 18 'Autoencoder Architecture').
items.focus: Walk all four lines — centring x̄ = x − b_d, the encoding f = ReLU(W_e x̄ + b_e), the decoding x̂ = W_d f + b_d, and the loss L = mean over X of ‖x − x̂‖₂² + λ‖f‖₁. Give the reason for each term: MSE for reconstruction fidelity, λ‖f‖₁ to push activations toward zero and buy sparsity, and note the asymmetry the paper flags (MSE is a mean over vector elements, the L1 penalty a sum), that W_d has unit-norm columns, and that m ≥ n makes the hidden layer overcomplete.

items.caption: Computational proxy as a log-likelihood ratio log(P(s|context)/P(s)) (Section 3, estimated in Appendices 12.1–12.2).
items.focus: Explain that s is a string or token, P(s|context) its likelihood under the hypothesised context model (base64 as uniform over 64 characters, DNA as uniform over A/T/C/G), and P(s) its likelihood under the empirical dataset distribution, estimated as the unigram product ∏_{t∈s} p(t). Say why the ratio rather than the raw likelihood is the right score — it corrects for tokens that are simply common.

items.caption: Bayes-rule estimate P(s|Arabic) = P(Arabic|s)·P(s)/P(Arabic) for script features (Appendix 12.3).
items.focus: Cover each of the three terms and how each is estimated: P(Arabic|s) by Unicode-block detection (1 if all characters are in Arabic blocks such as U+0600–U+06FF, else 1e−10, and for partial-character tokens by sampling occurrences), P(s) by the unigram product, P(Arabic) by applying the same heuristic to a random dataset sample. Note the acknowledged failure mode: shared punctuation counts as non-Arabic.

items.caption: Attribution score f_i(t_j)·v_{i,t_{j+1}} and the attribution vector built from it (Section 5.3.1 footnote).
items.focus: Define f_i(t_j) as feature i's activation at token t_j, v_{ik} as feature i's logit weight on vocabulary token k, and t_{j+1} as the token that actually came next, so the product measures how much the feature helped predict the real continuation. Explain that stacking these over sampled datapoints gives the attribution vector, that it approximates gradient×activation, and that it ignores the softmax denominator and layer norm.

items.caption: Feature ablation, replacing x^j with x^j − f_i(x^j)·d_i (Appendix 13).
items.focus: Explain that the feature's own contribution is subtracted from the MLP activation at every token before completing the forward pass, and that the measured quantity is the resulting change in predicted log-likelihood of each later token — orange background marks activation, blue underline the ablation effect. Note this is a directional (not zero-) ablation, which is what makes the effect attributable to that one feature.

sectionGroups.hint: The conceptual frame and the claims the paper makes about what features are. Expect: polysemanticity and the neuron as the wrong unit of analysis; the superposition hypothesis and noisy simulation of a larger sparser network; features as directions and the linear decomposition; the privileged basis; the four desiderata for a good decomposition (interpretable activation conditions, interpretable downstream effects, explaining a large fraction of the layer, causal relevance); why architectural sparsity approaches fail; and then the phenomenology this frame predicts — feature motifs, feature splitting as dictionary size grows, universality across independently trained models, and emergent 'finite state automata' where features' logit outputs re-trigger one another. Also the theoretical caveats in Discussion: feature manifolds and non-1-D structure, whether 'token in context' features are real, and the relation to prior dictionary-learning, disentanglement and superposition literature. The author-contributions and acknowledgments files carry no concepts and should be read only for attribution.

The machinery: how the sparse autoencoder is built, trained, and how everything is measured. Expect the encoder/decoder architecture with tied pre-encoder and post-decoder bias, the MSE + λ·L1 objective, unit-norm dictionary columns, overcompleteness and expansion factor (1× to 256× of the 512-neuron MLP), the one-layer transformer being studied and its Pile preprocessing, the 8-billion-activation training set sampled without replacement, Adam with 1M steps, and every training trick with its justification: pre-encoder bias initialized to the geometric median, untied decoder weights, dead-neuron resampling, learning-rate sweep, and the Adam/decoder-normalization gradient-projection fix. Also the measurement apparatus: the A/1/3450 run-and-feature notation, the feature and data-oriented visualization interfaces, the UMAP embedding procedure, the log-likelihood-ratio computational proxies and how P(s), P(s|base64) and P(s|Arabic) are each estimated, directional feature ablation, and the 0–3 human interpretability rubric. The hyperparameter-selection appendix carries the L0-vs-reconstructed-NLL Pareto tradeoff used to pick λ.

The evidence. Expect the four-part template applied to each case study (Arabic script A/1/3450, DNA A/1/2937, base64 A/1/2357, Hebrew A/1/416): activation specificity against the proxy, activation sensitivity, downstream effect via logit weights and ablation and pinned-feature sampling, the demonstration that no neuron matches the feature, and the correlated match in independently trained run B (correlations 0.85–0.92). Then the global claims: 412 manually rated features vs neurons, automated interpretability with Claude scored on activations and on logit weights, activation-interval analysis showing interpretability falls at weak activations, the caveats, and the headline 79% of the MLP's log-likelihood loss reduction recovered by A/1 features (94.5% for A/5 with 131,072 features) plus why that number should be read cautiously. Also the model-vs-data question via pinned sampling, the bimodal feature-density histograms and the ultralow-density/dead-neuron cluster, and the automated-interpretability appendix controls: Spearman setup, the randomized-transformer baseline with its single-token and positional modes, importance scoring and how its reweighting collapses feature scores toward zero, and the explanation-length null result.
